newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Jordan says price stability diagnosis tricky.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Jordan says price stability diagnosis tricky.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Jerry Jordan said on Tuesday the notion of price stability does not account for cyclical nor strutural changes in the U.S. economy.
"Price stability is a notion that means the economy won't change," Jordan told Reuters.
Jordan, a proponent of transparency at the Fed, said the U.S. central bank should be clear about its objectives and convey the message to the American people and financial markets.

Jordan, who spoke to Reuters after addressing a Consumer Bankers Association conference, said Americans would be baffled if asked "should the objective of monetary policy be zero-percent inflation or price stability."
The Cleveland Fed president said he prefers to define his monetary policy's objective as aiming at preserving the dollar's purchasing value.

"My goal is to plant in the mind of people the idea the purchasing power of the dollar in the future would be about the same as it is today," Jordan said, stressing he is referring to the purchasing power of the dollar -- not its exchange rate.
But Jordan said the debate about how close the U.S. central bank is from actual price stability is "a nice problem for the Fed to have" after years of a tough anti-inflation fight.
However, Jordan also stressed it is difficult for the Fed to know when it has achieved price stability or the steady purchasing power of the dollar -- because these are notions difficult to quantify.

"Because this is an idea, I have difficulties finding out what people are thinking about this may affect their decisions in the future," Jordan said. "There often is a disparity (in inflation expectations) between Wall Street and Main Street."
Asked whether he or the Fed feel they have achieved price stability, Jordan answered, "There is no single statistical index that I can look at to get the answer to that question."

Jordan, cautioning against financial markets' over-reaction to statistics, added "distinguishing between a data series and people's behavior is difficult to communicate if we are constantly asked if these data are too cold or too warm."
Jordan said the traditional market approach of looking at data to gauge the performance of the economy is outdated.
"We're using 19th-century measures to try to transcribe the behavior of 20th-century people," he said.

The Cleveland Fed president said the "Fed has access to a tremendous amount of information that does not turn up in data series," citing the anecdotal information contained in the Beige Book prepared for discussion at Federal Open Market Committee meetings.

Jordan, though he supported the preemptive monetary policy principle, acknowledged "the problem with anticipatory monetary policy is that not only we -- but everybody else -- is going to find out only later on whether it was the right move."
